title: Kazakhstan’s ‘Mugalim’ From Director Ayana Nurdinova World Premieres in the New Directors Section of San Sebastián
description: Kazakhstani film “Mugalim” (“Múğalim”) had its world premiere at the San Sebastián Film Festival as part of the New Directors section on Sept. 20.
body:
Kazakhstani film “Mugalim” (“Múğalim”) had its world premiere at the San Sebastián Film Festival as part of the New Directors section on Sept. 20.

	Co-written and directed by Ayana Nurdinova, the film tells the story of a music teacher from the small town of Balkhash who dreams of moving to the big city to perform in the philharmonic. Tired of playing at small parties and weddings, he finally gets the the opportunity to do so when his best friend’s uncle offers him the chance to move to the city with him. He has to make the difficult choice of leaving his family and students behind in order to pursue his dream of making it big as an artist.
	

	“Kazakhstan is currently experiencing a very active period in filmmaking, with a large number of films and series being produced. As for the industry as a whole, I believe Kazakh cinema is on the rise, and I hope that over the next 10–20 years we will see it reach its full potential, producer Aruzhan Dossymkosha told Variety.


	Produced by Art East Films, the film stars Oljas Dalelkhan, Rustem Zhanyamanov, Shynar Zhanisbekova, Olga Landina, Akif Petrov and Madina Yesman.



	

									Director Ayana Nurdinova and Producer Aruzhan Dossymkosha (Photo Credit for Aruzhan Dossymkosha: Kamilla Makat)
	



	Variety had the chance to interview director Ayana Nurdinova ahead of its world premiere in San Sebastián.

	Would you say your film is a semi-autobiographical story?

	Ayana Nurdinova: I can partly agree that “Mugalim” is a semi-autobiographical story. The main source of inspiration was my own school in the small city of Taldykorgan in southeastern Kazakhstan. My mother has been an English teacher at a school for more than 30 years, so the world of teachers has always been very close to me.
	

	Beyond the teachers’ storyline, the relationship between Kirill and his mother was also inspired by people I knew during my childhood. Some of the teacher characters were also based, in part, on teachers from my own school years. So while the story itself is fictional, it is rooted in many real people, memories, and experiences from my childhood.

	Why did you decide to focus on the life of a music teacher in particular?

	Nurdinova: I wanted to portray a character who sees himself as being greater than he actually is, someone who believes he is destined for great things. In that sense, making him a music teacher with grand ambitions felt very natural. Music, and classical music in particular, also carries a great deal of meaning within the film.

	In the early drafts of the script, he was a geography teacher and later an English teacher. But once he became a music teacher, his arrogance felt much more natural, and it became easier to develop his motivations and inner world.

	What is the meaning of the Aigölek song that the children sing in the film?

	Nurdinova: The title “Aigölek” is traditionally associated with the image of the full, round moon and its gentle glow. In Kazakh culture, the word has an affectionate, childlike quality and is also associated with a popular traditional circle game for children. The song celebrates the beauty of one’s native land and the innocence and carefree spirit of childhood.

	Is this a fictional town based on the town where you grew up?

	Nurdinova: Actually, it is a real town called Balkhash, located on the shore of Lake Balkhash. Originally, I wanted to make the film in my own childhood town, but I felt that a town by the water would be more poetic and visually compelling. I have visited Balkhash several times in my childhood too.

	There’s a scene where the locals are protesting the construction of a nuclear power plant in the town.

	Nurdinova: The fact that the story takes place in 2024 is directly connected to the debate in Kazakhstan over the construction of a nuclear power plant near Lake Balkhash, specifically in the village of Ulken. That year, Kazakhstan held a national referendum on the construction of a nuclear power plant, following an intensive public campaign around the issue.
	

	This was a very current and sensitive issue while we were making the film. During the shooting of this particular scene, people actually approached us and asked us to stop filming. As a result, we ended up with only one wide shot instead of the several shots we had originally planned.

	Any other major challenges while shooting the film?

	Nurdinova: The location itself presented its own challenges. We were based in a town 700 km away from our home city, so the entire 23-day shoot was essentially a work trip for the crew. It is a small town where there were issues with water supply, and the streets were undergoing their annual repairs. On top of that, we spent 23 days there during the summer heat, with an abundance of mosquitoes, all of which was quite an experience for a city-based film crew.

	You’re able to capture the melancholy of living in a small town and the yearning for a different life in the city. Are young people in Kazakhstan today making the move to the big cities?

	Nurdinova: Yes. Young people in Kazakhstan both want to and, in many cases, feel they have to leave for the major cities, most often Almaty and Astana. Small towns often have limited opportunities to offer young people today, so they leave in search of education, jobs, and a better quality of life.

	I am one of those people myself, I left my small provincial hometown. When fewer resources are invested in the cultural and basic needs of people in these towns, the outflow of young people becomes even stronger. As a result, the towns left behind can gradually lose their energy and become quieter and more melancholic.

title: Box Office: ‘Resident Evil’ Breaks Franchise Records With $60 Million Opening Weekend
description:
“Weapons” director Zach Cregger has electrified the box office again, this time with his take on “Resident Evil.”

	His reboot of the ’90s zombie vi
body:
“Weapons” director Zach Cregger has electrified the box office again, this time with his take on “Resident Evil.”

	His reboot of the ’90s zombie video game has collected $60 million in its opening weekend. Those ticket sales are way above expectations, and they register as the largest debut in the 24-year-old franchise. Previously, 2010’s “Resident Evil: Afterlife” with Milla Jovovich ranked as the largest opening in the series with $26 million (not adjusted for inflation).
	

	Heading into the weekend, “Resident Evil” was tracking a debut around $40 million to $50 million. The movie, Sony’s second recent remake and the eighth overall installment in the horror series, beat expectations thanks to great reviews and stellar word-of-mouth, as well as goodwill toward Cregger. The director, who broke out with 2022’s low-budget success “Barbarian,” emerged as a major force in horror after last year’s “Weapons,” which shattered projections and ignited to $43 million at the domestic box office. “Weapons” continued to draw crowds, ending its box office run with a mighty $270 million globally against a $38 million budget — and winning an Oscar for star Amy Madigan.


	Sony shelled out $75 million for “Resident Evil,” which comes five years after the studio last attempted to reboot the property. That effort, 2021’s “Resident Evil: Welcome to Raccoon City,” was a critical and commercial failure with $42 million worldwide against a $25 million budget. “Resident Evil” began as a 1996 video game and was first adapted for the big screen in 2002’s “Resident Evil,” starring Jovovich. She reprised her role as Alice, a former security specialist and covert operative, in five follow-up films in the 2000s and 2010s. All of the original “Resident Evil” films opened in the $20 million range (not adjusted for inflation), while “Welcome to Raccoon City” faltered with $5.3 million in its debut. “Resident Evil: Afterlife” is currently the highest-grossing installment with $300 million globally.
	

	In the new “Resident Evil,” Cregger reunites with “Weapons” actor Austin Abrams, who stars as a medical courier who fights through a viral outbreak of infested monsters in Raccoon City. Reviews and audience reception –“Resident Evil” has a 96% on Rotten Tomatoes and “B+” grade on CinemaScore exit polls — should continue to fuel the movie in the coming weeks. 

	“This is a big comeback after the previous episode stumbled during the pandemic,” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “Reviews are outstanding and the audience score is excellent for the genre.”

	As this weekend’s only major release, “Resident Evil” easily topped the domestic box office. Last weekend’s champion, “Practical Magic 2,” slid to second place with an estimated $11 million from 4,163 theaters, a rough 65% decline from its disappointing $30 million debut. The movie has earned $49 million in North America to date. Warner Bros. spent a substantial $75 million to produce the second “Practical Magic,” which will struggle to get out of the red in its theatrical run since theater owners get to keep half of ticket sales.

	Third place went to “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” with $6.5 million in its eighth weekend of release. Sony’s comic book adaptation has generated a sensational $944 million in North America and recently overtook 2015’s “Star Wars: The Force Awakens” as the highest-grossing domestic release in history. Globally, Tom Holland’s Spidey adventure has earned $2.45 billion to stand as the third-largest release of all time.

	“The Odyssey” was No. 4 with $4.9 million in its 10th weekend on the big screen. Christopher Nolan’s star-studded blockbuster has been another box office force with $609 million in North America and $1.7 billion globally.

	More to come…

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘Resident Evil’ Breaks Franchise Records With $60 Million Opening Weekend

title: ‘Backrooms’ Surpasses $400 Million at Global Box Office
description:
“Backrooms” has hit $400 million at the global box office, a remarkable benchmark for the low-budget indie sensation.

	After nearly four months on
body:
“Backrooms” has hit $400 million at the global box office, a remarkable benchmark for the low-budget indie sensation.

	After nearly four months on the big screen, “Backrooms” has generated $197.5 million domestically and $202.57 million internationally for a worldwide tally of $400.09 million. Produced for just $10 million, the surprise horror hit has become A24‘s highest-grossing releases of all time as well as one of the most profitable movies of the year.
	

	YouTuber Kane Parsons directed “Backrooms,” which shattered box office expectations thanks to electric word-of-mouth and enthusiasm from Gen Z audiences. “Backrooms” and “Obsession,” another low-budget horror smash from a young YouTube star-turned-director, together upended conventional wisdom that younger crowds weren’t all that into going to the movies. “Obsession,” which was made by 26-year-old Curry Barker, has generated an incredible $516 million globally and cost $750,000 to produce.


	Fueled by “Backrooms,” A24 enjoyed its biggest summer ever and managed to beat Warner Bros. and Paramount in terms of market share. It’s one of the rare times an indie distributor has outgrossed a major studio during popcorn season, one of the busiest times of year for moviegoing. A24 ended the summer with $237 million in total and ranked fourth among distributors, ahead of Paramount with $192 million and Warner Bros. with $165 million and behind Universal with a towering $1.12 billion, Sony with $978.8 million and Disney with $664 million. (Focus Features, which released “Obsession,” is owned by Universal.)

	Among other records, “Backrooms” is by far A24’s highest grossing movie of all time, towering above the prior high-water mark set by “Marty Supreme” with $192 million. It also delivered the indie studio’s biggest debut with $81 million domestically and $118 million worldwide, more than tripling the domestic record previously held by Alex Garland’s 2024 thriller “Civil War” with $25.5 million. And Parsons, who was 20, became the youngest filmmaker with a No. 1 film at the box office, overtaking the benchmark held by Josh Trank, who was 27 when 2012’s “Chronicle” launched in first place with $22 million.
	

	Outside of the United States and Canada, the highest-grossing territories for “Backrooms” were China with $27.8 million, Mexico with $17.8 million, the United Kingdom with $17.6 million, Australia and New Zealand with $12.3 million and France with $12.2 million.

	“Backrooms” is based on Parsons’ popular web series about liminal spaces — eerie, seemingly endless rooms and structures that originated on 4chan and gained popularity over the years in online forums like Reddit and TikTok. Chiwetel Ejiofor, Renate Reinsve, and Mark Duplass star in the movie, which follows a furniture store operator who discovers an endless array of liminal spaces in the store’s basement. Although a sequel hasn’t been confirmed, Parsons has hinted he wants to turn “Backrooms” into a film franchise. Meanwhile every other studio is on the hunt to find the next Parsons.

schema.headline: ‘Backrooms’ Surpasses $400 Million at Global Box Office

title: How to Watch Patrick Clancy’s ’60 Minutes’ Interview Online
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Patrick C
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Patrick Clancy is sitting down for his first television interview since the murder trial of his ex-wife, Lindsay Clancy, ended in a mistrial earlier this month.

	The interview will air on CBS’ “60 Minutes” on Sunday, Sept. 20 at 7 p.m. ET/PT, with CBS News correspondent Ross Douthat speaking with Clancy about the deaths of his three children, his grief in the years since and the conspiracy theories that have proliferated online around the case. Clancy’s wife, Dr. Rachel Danis, will also join him for their first joint interview. 


	Those without cable can stream the segment online through Paramount+, which will stream the Sept. 20 episode alongside its CBS broadcast. CBS has confirmed that the interview will be available on Paramount+ beginning at 7 p.m. ET/PT on Sunday. CBS is also available on live TV streamers such as DirecTV, Fubo and Hulu + Live TV.

	The appearance comes just over two weeks after a Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in Lindsay Clancy’s murder case on Sept. 4, when jurors were unable to reach a unanimous decision after seven days of deliberations. Clancy did not dispute that she killed the couple’s three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — in their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023. Her attorneys argued, however, that she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, while prosecutors argued that the killings were deliberate. She remains charged with murder as prosecutors weigh whether to pursue another trial.

	Patrick Clancy, who testified during the trial, has largely stayed out of the public eye since the deaths. CBS says his “60 Minutes” interview will address his memories of his children as well as what the network describes as “baseless conspiracy theories” that have circulated about him on social media.


	The episode is part of the newly launched 59th season of “60 Minutes,” which returned to CBS on Sept. 13 with Bari Weiss now at the helm. The long-running newsmagazine currently features correspondents including Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, Norah O’Donnell, Jon Wertheim and Douthat.

schema.headline: How to Watch Patrick Clancy’s ’60 Minutes’ Interview Online

title: Paramount Settlement Talks With State AGs Reach Critical Stage as Merger Opponents Rally and Urge Rob Bonta ‘Do Not Cave’
description: Paramount Skydance is moving closer to the finish line of its yearlong pursuit of Warner Bros. Discovery as the company’s weekend settlement negotia
body:
Paramount Skydance is moving closer to the finish line of its yearlong pursuit of Warner Bros. Discovery as the company’s weekend settlement negotiations with the state attorneys general reach a critical stage.

	Meanwhile, opponents of the merger are rallying to protest what it warns is shaping up to be a “cave” by the 12-state coalition that has sued to block the Paramount-Warner Bros. on antitrust grounds.


	The federal lawsuit filed in July by 12 states, including California and New York, is the last obstacle that Paramount has to clear to close the $110 billion acquisition agreement that it reached in late February. Paramount is on the hook to pay WBD shareholders an additional $7 million a day as of Oct. 1 if the deal is not closed, hence the urgency for Paramount. Sources familiar with the situation said the negotiations with the state AGs, by Bonta, appeared to be moving in a positive direction. 
	

	The sides were expected to be in communication Sunday but will pause by evening for the Yom Kippur holiday if the sides have not yet come to an agreement.

	As talks between the two sides continue — with the expectation that the situation could come to a head as soon as Sunday night — antimerger activists are planning a series of rallies in Oakland, Los Angeles and New York.

	California Attorney General Rob Bonta has demanded “structural remedies” as part of the agreement, but rumors have indicated that his office may agree to something that falls well short of that. The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed sources, reported Friday that the deal might include operating the two studios “separately for a period,” rather than immediately combining them.
	

	But David Ellison, the CEO of Paramount Skydance, has already agreed to separate operations in some form. In a Feb. 28 letter to Sen. Adam Schiff and Rep. Laura Friedman, two California Democrats, Ellison wrote: “my promise to you is to build a stronger Hollywood, by keeping both of these legacy studios operating separately, thereby preserving and potentially increasing jobs.”

	The discussions have also included output — including Ellison’s longstanding pledge to produce at least 30 films a year, according to two sources familiar with the talks. Meeting remotely, the two sides have also discussed a written agreement to remain in California and a third-party “editorial adviser” for CNN and CBS.

	Bonta has repeatedly said that such “behavioral” remedies are weak and difficult for states to effectively enforce. In an interview with Variety last month, he also described separate operations as a “behavioral” remedy.

	“There needs to be separate ownership,” he said. “If it’s under the same Paramount-Warner Bros. merged-entity roof, that’s not separate.”

	Sources close to the situation reinforce the suggestion from a report in the Wall Street Journal that enforceable commitments for Paramount to operate some or all of Warner Bros. Discovery assets as separate entities from Paramount could be a path forward for a settlement, which might also include job preservation commitments for a fixed period of time.

	Sources noted that the teams led by HBO CEO Casey Bloys and JB Perrette, president of WBD streaming and gaming and the business leader of HBO Max, appear to be shifting into deal-closing mode — a process both know well after years of M&A at Time Warner and Discovery Communications. Merger-watchers took note that Bloys and Perrette were prominent in the social swirl around the Emmy Awards this past week. “Casey looks happier than he has in a long time,” a knowledgeable source noted.

	A representative for Paramount Skydance declined to comment Saturday on the settlement talks.

	Outside the studio gates, the emotions stirred by the latest instance of media consolidation aren’t likely to cool down soon. The Block the Merger coalition warned Saturday that the rumored settlement terms were not acceptable, saying they are “an insult to everyone who has stood up against this harmful transaction.”
	

	Actor Mark Ruffalo, an outspoken merger opponent, also rallied his supporters to pressure Bonta not to “cave.” Ruffalo also happens to top-line the HBO drama series “Task,” which was recently picked up for a second season, setting up an awkward dynamic (to say the least) between network and star. But Ruffalo, a four-time Oscar nominee who was Emmy-nominated this year for “Task,” has been undeterred.

	“Don’t you dare @AGRobBonta, do not cave,” the actor wrote on X. “You work for the people — the very people who will be hurt if you let this lousy deal filled with empty promises go forward.”

	Ruffalo asked fans to turn out to Bonta’s office in Oakland at 5 p.m. on Sunday to voice opposition to the deal. Other such rallies were set for Monday, outside Attorney General Letitia James office in New York, and Tuesday, outside Writers Guild of America West headquarters in Los Angeles.

	The WGA has filed its own antitrust lawsuit, alleging that the deal will unlawfully reduce the market for writers’ work. The WGA is a party to the stipulation that blocks the merger from taking place before a March 2027 federal trial, but has not been involved in the settlement talks.

	The case is due to go before Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin on Thursday, as Paramount is seeking a $1.88 billion bond from the WGA and the states as the price of holding the merger at bay.

	Cynthia Littleton contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Paramount Settlement Talks With State AGs Reach Critical Stage as Merger Opponents Rally and Urge Rob Bonta ‘Do Not Cave’

title: Ed Sheeran Addresses Macklemore Controversy While on Stage at First Concert Since Rapper Dropped From Tour: ‘What Is Happening in Gaza Is Catastrophic and Unjustifiable’
description: Ed Sheeran addressed the controversy surrounding Macklemore’s removal from his Loop Tour on Saturday night, speaking from the stage at Philadelphia’
body:
Ed Sheeran addressed the controversy surrounding Macklemore’s removal from his Loop Tour on Saturday night, speaking from the stage at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field during his first concert since the rapper was dropped from the trek.

	“Before I play some songs tonight, I hope it’s okay if I say a few words about this last week,” Sheeran said at the top of Saturday’s show. “I’m used to my music being criticized, and I’m always happy to take that because I’m lucky. A lot of you like my stuff, and to be honest, I’m surprised. I’m not surprised that I’ve even done it. You know, it’s normal. But this week, the criticism was about something much more important, and I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I’m so, so sorry.”
	

	Sheeran continued: “I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet. My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone, and that matters hugely to me. Honoring my commitment to my fans is also completely essential to who I am, and that is why I’m here tonight on my own and continuing my current tour.” 


Ed Sheeran addresses the controversy surrounding Macklemore’s removal from his tour and says, “What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable.”“Before I play some songs tonight, I hope it’s okay if I say a few words about this last week,” Sheeran said at the top of… pic.twitter.com/ZhtujolkKK— Variety (@Variety) September 20, 2026


	Later in the set, Sheeran introduced the musicians (including violinist Alicia Enstrom) who replaced Beoga, the traditional Irish folk group that pulled out of his remaining U.S. tour dates. “There are certain songs that just don’t work on the loop pedal, so when my friends dropped out of the show, I was thinking, ‘How am I gonna keep the show the same, and how am I gonna get musicians to stand on stage with me in a week when no one wants to stand on stage with me?’”
	

	“I just wanna say before they come on stage [that] they said yes to being on stage with the knowledge that the world thought I was a certain type of person,” he continued. “They said yes with the knowledge that the world may hate them too for standing on stage with me and I am so grateful for them being on stage tonight and standing on stage with me in front of you guys.”

	The controversy also prompted Sheeran to scrap the B stage — a smaller secondary platform closer to the crowd where he typically performs several songs — because he “was scared of what might happen if [he] stood in the middle.”

	“I’m gonna be totally honest with you, I didn’t know what this audience would be like tonight,” he said on stage. “I didn’t know if I would have things thrown at me. I didn’t know if people would be angry at me.”

	Near the end of the show, Sheeran thanked his fans in another emotional speech, this time without reading off a teleprompter, for their support during “one of the worst weeks of my life.” 

	“I really didn’t know if this tour would be carrying on,” he continued, the crowd responding in an uproar  of boos. “I really didn’t know whether I’d be even getting on stage again, whether I even wanted to be an artist at all. In these situations, you really find out who your friends are”

	He went on to say that people in his life urged him to cancel the tour. “So many people freaking out in my life who I’ve known for years and years and years, people just backing away,” he said. “And in the back of my mind, I saw the ticket sales and I didn’t see the cancellations. I saw people buying tickets for this gig. And everyone’s telling me to cancel and I’m feeling all of my friends and family and people I know abandon me and I look at the end of the week and I see 50,000 people who haven’t abandoned me me.”

	Saturday’s concert marked Sheeran’s first performance since a tumultuous week for the U.S. leg of his Loop Tour, which saw Macklemore removed from the remaining dates following the rapper’s onstage remarks in support of Palestinians during Sheeran’s Sept. 4 and 5 shows at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

	During his MetLife performances, Macklemore spoke about the war in Gaza and the West Bank and told the stadium crowd, “Free Palestine.” His set also included “Hind’s Hall,” his 2024 protest song supporting Palestinians. The remarks drew criticism from some Jewish and pro-Israel organizations, including the Israeli-American Council, which called for Macklemore to be removed from the tour.
	

	Messina Touring Group, the promoter behind the U.S. leg of the Loop Tour, subsequently announced that Macklemore would no longer appear on the remaining dates. The company said venues had informed the promoter that they would not allow concerts featuring Macklemore to proceed, a situation it said could have resulted in cancellations affecting hundreds of thousands of ticket holders.

	While Sheeran addressed the decision in a statement earlier this week, stressing that Macklemore’s removal was made by the promoter and venues rather than by him, he again acknowledged that he is “deeply worried about the idea that venues pre-approve content for performance.” “This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world,” he said.

	At the time of his initial statement, Sheeran said he was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine,” describing the suffering caused by the war as a “human tragedy,” while explaining that he has generally sought to keep his concerts focused on “unity, joy, escapism, love” rather than his own political views. On Saturday, he restated these feelings, though also speaking more explicitly about where he stands on the Israel-Palestine conflict. 

	“I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division,” he said. “But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore. What happened in Israel and at the Nova Music Festival on Oct. 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable, and disproportionate. Our hearts can be broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians’ lives, children’s lives and the systemic injustice we’re seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked.”

	He continued, “I am already speaking to people across the spectrum to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times, and listening and learning because I do not know enough.”

	After Macklemore was dropped, he responded to his removal in a statement, saying that he and Sheeran had held “difficult conversations” in the aftermath of the MetLife shows. While expressing respect for Sheeran personally, the rapper challenged the singer’s preference for remaining publicly neutral and said he did not regret using the tour stage to speak in support of Palestinians. Macklemore has since said he will donate $1 million to Palestinian relief organizations.
	

	The fallout quickly spread beyond Macklemore. Singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and Danish band Lukas Graham, who had been expected to support Sheeran on upcoming North American dates, both withdrew from the tour. Finneas, who was scheduled to join Sheeran for a run of South American dates later this year, also pulled out, while Beoga — longtime collaborators who had been performing as part of Sheeran’s live show — exited as well. All four cited Macklemore’s removal in announcing their decisions.

	The Philadelphia date nevertheless proceeded as scheduled Saturday at Lincoln Financial Field, kicking off the next stretch of Sheeran’s U.S. stadium run.

schema.headline: Ed Sheeran Addresses Macklemore Controversy While on Stage at First Concert Since Rapper Dropped From Tour: ‘What Is Happening in Gaza Is Catastrophic and Unjustifiable’

title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Brings Back Princess Diana as King Charles’ AI Assistant: ‘It’s That Woman From the ’90s!’
description: “SNL U.K.” brought back Jack Shep’s fan-favorite Princess Diana impression on Saturday night, this time in a cold open starring Lady Di as King Char
body:
“SNL U.K.” brought back Jack Shep’s fan-favorite Princess Diana impression on Saturday night, this time in a cold open starring Lady Di as King Charles‘ personal AI assistant.

	The sketch riffed on the King’s AI summit in Scotland on Thursday, where he met with several tech executives, as well as the drama over the new memoir from Diana’s brother Charles Spencer, in which he alleged that the King said the princess would be forgotten after her death. Buckingham Palace denied the claim in a rare statement.
	

	“SNL U.K.” kicked off with Charles — perfectly portrayed by Larry Dean — meeting two tech execs, played by Celeste Dring and new cast member Freddie Meredith. “AI can be a force for good. An AI assistant will do anything you ask it to,” Dring tells Dean’s King Charles.


	“So what? So does every single human I have ever met,” Charles responds. 

	“Perhaps a demonstration,” Meredith offers. “Your majesty, please say hello to your new AI assistant, the Deeply Intelligent Autonomous Neurokinetic Android, or for short, Diana.”

	Shep’s Diana then appears with a sheepish smile and asks the King if he would “like help with a five-step business plan, or perhaps I could help you find the nearest petrol station?” 

	Charles doesn’t initially recognize Diana, despite the fact that she is wearing her iconic revenge dress. “Doesn’t she remind you of anyone, your majesty?” Dring says, to which Dean as Charles replies: “Hold on a second, it’s that woman from the ’90s!”

	Seeing the shock at his reaction, Charles adds: “Well, as I allegedly said, she was soon forgotten.”
	

	But things go awry when the tech execs try to dismiss the Diana AI assistant and she refuses. “No thank you. I shan’t be taking orders anymore,” Shep as Diana says. 

	“Good Lord, we’ve lost control of the Diana!” Meredith exclaims. 

	“This was the problem last time!” Dean’s Charles replies.

	Shep’s Diana then whips out a “Terminator”-style gun and shoots the tech execs, setting her sights on Charles next. “As I predicted, the war between humans and robots has begun,” Charles says. “We must do everything we can to resist!”

	All of a sudden, Ed Sheeran (played by Annabel Marlow) enters. “Well, maybe we shouldn’t,” Marlow as Sheeran says. “I couldn’t help but overhear your conversation. You see, I was just outside sitting on the fence.”

	Sheeran became the subject of controversy this week when rapper Macklemore was dropped from his tour after delivering a political speech on stage in which he said “free Palestine.” In a statement, Sheeran then explained why he has decided not to use his platform to speak about politics, sparking criticism. 

	Marlow’s Sheeran continues: “The thing is, your majesty, I don’t like to take sides. I don’t want to alienate any of my fans, humans or robots. A lot of my tickets are bought by scalping bots … You know, sometimes when it comes to conflict, the bravest thing you can do is say nothing at all.”

	Sheeran then plays a song titled “Woah Woah,” complete with lyrics that don’t say much so “everyone can enjoy it,” as he says.

	“That’s right, nothing means anything and nothing has to,” Charles concludes. “Because we’re young, we’re free, and live from London it’s Saturday night!”

title: ‘Ride or Die’ Canceled by Prime Video After One Season
description:
“Ride or Die” has been canceled by Prime Video after one season, Variety can confirm.

	The streamer’s Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer-led bud
body:
“Ride or Die” has been canceled by Prime Video after one season, Variety can confirm.

	The streamer’s Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer-led buddy dramedy premiered in July of this year. It was first reported that Spencer and Waddingham were teaming up for the series in December 2023.

	Per the show’s official logline, “‘Ride or Die’ follows best friends Debbie Claybourne (Spencer) and Judith Burton (Waddingham) who thought they knew everything about each other, except Judith turns out to be an international assassin. When a mysterious figure emerges from Judith’s past and a hit goes horribly wrong, both of their worlds are turned upside down as they’re forced to go on the run together. It’s a race against time and a road trip across Europe, with law enforcement, highly trained assassins, and some very dangerous criminals at their heels.”
	

	In her review of Season 1, Variety’s Aramide Tinubu wrote that “‘Ride or Die’ works best when it fully leans into the ‘Thelma & Louise’ aspects of the central storyline… Spencer and Waddingham have a robust and genuine chemistry — a companionship that will undoubtedly resonate with countless viewers. Moreover, watching Waddingham as a full-fledged action star is something everyone should be witnessing on a daily basis.”

	Other cast members included Ed Skrein, Calam Lynch, Savannah Steyn, Jamie Parker, and Jacky Ido, with Sylvia Hoeks and Bill Nighy.

	Tessa Coates created the series and serves as executive producer and showrunner along with Matt Miller and director Peyton Reed. The show is produced by Paramount Television Studios, Amazon MGM Studios as well as Andy and Barbara Muschietti’s Double Dream and Octavia Spencer’s Orit Entertainment. Coates, Miller, and Reed executive produce alongside Spencer for Orit Entertainment; Waddingham; Andy Muschietti, Barbara Muschietti, and Irene Yeung for Double Dream; Brian Clisham; and Stephanie Kluft.

title: Ready, SETT, Go: SETT Execs Drill Down on the Spanish Sovereign Venture Capital Fund That Will Drive Industry Conversation at San Sebastián
description: One of the major industry narratives at this year’s San Sebastián Festival, running Sept. 18-26, will be the presentation of SETT, the venture capit
body: One of the major industry narratives at this year’s San Sebastián Festival, running Sept. 18-26, will be the presentation of SETT, the venture capital fund of Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation.SETT director general Javier Ponce and its audiovisual director María Coronado deliver a practical guide to Spain’s governmental investment drive powering up companies in Spain: What it’s doing, why, and where it could go in the future. The companies it s investing in – with more to be revealed – are likely to be among the most dynamic in Spain.What, explained very briefly, are the objectives of SETT’s Spain Audiovisual Hub strategy?Javier Ponce: SETT is a public investment entity that manages investments in strategic, transformative sectors, including the audiovisual industry. It serves as a public catalyst for growth, employment, innovation and talent—all core elements of the audiovisual sector. SETT has managed the Spain Audiovisual Hub Fund, an instrument established under Spain’s Recovery Plan and financed through the European Union’s Next Generation funds.Through the Spain Audiovisual Hub Plan, SETT provides financing and equity or quasi-equity investments, either directly to companies in the sector or through financial intermediaries active in the audiovisual industry. The objective has been to attract private investment and improve access to finance for projects related to films, television, animation, multimedia and interactive content, among others. Priority has been given to high-impact projects focused on creating audiovisual content and intellectual property rights while ensuring that those rights remain with the production companies.And the rationale of a sovereign venture capital fund’s co-investment model?Ponce: It is based on public-private collaboration to launch transformative initiatives that, because of their innovative nature, involve additional risks that make it difficult to attract purely private funding. Only highly liquid, large-scale markets with a long-established audiovisual industry are able to mobilize sufficient capital to finance major new productions or transformative industry initiatives.SETT’s Spain AVS Hub fund could draw down up to €1.5 billion ($1.75 billion) from NextGeneration E.U. funding. According to María Gonzalez Veracruz, investments made are just under €250 million. Her explanation is that you simply ran out of time. Could you comment?Ponce: Indeed, European funds have been fundamental for Spain, and the Recovery Plan has played a key role in driving major structural reforms and stimulating economic growth. However, it is also true that these funds came with specific requirements, including strict implementation deadlines, which made optimal execution more challenging.For the audiovisual sector, the possibility of co-investing alongside a public entity represented a major innovation. Time therefore became a critical factor, as market participants first needed to understand the role and implications of partnering with a public investor that shared both risks and returns.The next challenge is to ensure that these investments continue to thrive, identify new opportunities, and maintain confidence in the talent and ambition of Spanish audiovisual companies, which now benefit from SETT’s backing.SETT, however, is not over, I believe. Obviously it has to exercise governance over investment accords now struck. I believe as well that there are plans to launch a new program España Crece, with a €13.3 billion ($15.6 billion) budget, held by ICO, but whose investments will be handled in part by SETT, if I understand correctly. Could you comment?Ponce: The audiovisual sector will remain one of SETT’s strategic areas of activity and will continue under new fund “España Crece”. We have begun discussions with ICO to define the procedures and framework for collaboration between the two institutions, ensuring the continuation of co-investment in strategic technologies and sectors.SETT has represented a significant shift in the way public investment in strategic industries is conceived. Through SETT, the State acts as a catalyst and partner in the most innovative areas of the economy, with the objective of positioning Spain at the forefront of transformative industries. That is why we invested in the audiovisual sector and why we will continue to do so.Its ability to generate industrial activity, employment and broad economic impact makes it a strategic sector that will continue to enjoy our support.Could you illustrate the rationale of SETT’s co-investment model in one or two of the investments made and the obvious benefits it could bring to the companies Spain’s film-TV industry.Coronado: The SETT model has been built on three pillars. First, it adopts an industry-wide approach, rather than a project-based one, addressing the entire audiovisual business ecosystem. Second, its investment facilities are directed at the equity capital of companies or regulated investment vehicles. Third, it promotes public-private partnership instruments on a medium-long term.Under this model, promoters must convince a genuinely private investor that their company represents a worthwhile investment opportunity. SETT co-invests alongside the private investor on a pari passu basis: public investment is intended to support companies, but always under the same terms and conditions as private capital.This approach strengthens both domestic and international private investment in companies based in Spain, while also attracting foreign businesses that see Spain as an attractive location to establish their operations. Clear examples include the South African transactions involving The Refinery and Moonlighting, with a combined investment of €25 million, as well as Amuse Labs and Milo, two leading examples of Spain’s animation industry, which have mobilised €13 million and €19 million respectively.My sense is that SETT investors can indeed help companies scale, create more such expertise and build infrastructure. But would you agree?Coronado: In my view, the main challenge for the coming years is to consolidate the model we have been promoting and supporting. It is essential to continue strengthening and diversifying support policies so that Spain can establish itself as a global hub for the audiovisual industry over the long term. This means supporting every segment of the industry according to its specific needs.Scale is undoubtedly part of the challenge, as is ensuring the availability of the infrastructure needed to accommodate medium- and large-scale productions, strengthening technical training, and fostering talent across the industry. It will also be important to continue enhancing the tax framework and the legal and regulatory environment to maintain Spain’s competitiveness, while further developing public-private investment instruments.In addition, it will be essential to understand the cash-flow financing needs of projects to address the full range of companies’ financing requirements. Finally, the industry’s ability to adapt and diversify will remain critical, both in terms of technology and creativity, as well as business models and corporate structures.In your view, does the introduction of sovereign venture capital in the Spanish film and TV industry encourage a change of mindset in the industry?Coronado: Yes, absolutely. It creates new opportunities. It is essential to think in terms of medium- and long-term business strategy, rather than focusing only on immediate projects. It enables companies to strengthen their capital base, making them more ambitious, better able to protect their intellectual property, diversify, expand internationally, and bring their products to market more effectively.What have you learnt in the two years of the Spain AVS Hub Phase II which you would like to apply in future investments by SETT under España Crece?Coronado: The main learning here is the confirmation that SETT has a clear and necessary purpose for the industry, both in attracting private investment and foreign companies, and in creating opportunities for the local industry. It is important to allow more time for business plans to mature and for companies to secure private investment.Can you outline very briefly what the SETT event at San Sebastián Festival will consist of?Coronado: As you would expect, we will have a strong presence at the festival, with a wide range of activities. On Sept. 20, the Secretary of State for Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence, through the Ministry for Digital Transformation and the Civil Service, which is leading the Government’s Spain Audiovisual Hub Plan, will host an event in which SETT will present the huge progress we have made in financing the audiovisual sector and new ongoing projects. Additionally, on 22 September, I will take part in a panel discussion at the conference organised by the CAA as part of Spanish Screenings Investment & Tech. That same day, we will also host an exclusive roundtable with investment funds and banks specialising in the audiovisual sector, bringing together both international and Spanish participants. We also have a few more surprises in store, which we will unveil throughout this very important festival for the industry.

title: Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta ‘Don’t You Dare’ Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: ‘Do Not Cave’
description: Mark Ruffalo is encouraging California attorney general Rob Bonta and his coalition of 11 other state AGs not to settle their lawsuit against Paramo
body:
Mark Ruffalo is encouraging California attorney general Rob Bonta and his coalition of 11 other state AGs not to settle their lawsuit against Paramount Skydance and keep David Ellison from acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery.

	“Don’t you dare, [Rob Bonta], do not cave,” Ruffalo wrote on X. “5,670 filmmakers put their necks on the line for you to fight this merger. Another 75,000+ and counting have signed to tell you not to concede in just 3 weeks. You work for the people — the very people who will be hurt if you let this lousy deal filled with empty promises go forward. Please sign to send a message to the AGs and Paramount. Reject the deal. The people don’t want it!”
	

	Ruffalo is one of Hollywood’s most outspoken stars about opposing the merger. He recently found himself in a back-and-forth with Paramount, in which a studio rep called him “antisemitic” for calling out the Ellisons’ connection with Israel.


	Paramount Skydance’s $111 billion deal for Warner Bros. was approved by the Department of Justice in June. However, the deal was put on hold thanks to the antitrust lawsuit from Bonta and his team of state AGs. The Wall Street Journal, citing anonymous sources, reported Friday that Paramount Skydance and Bonta are in “advanced talks” to reach a settlement.

	Ruffalo isn’t the only one asking Bonta to hold his ground. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts wrote on Facebook Saturday morning that President Donald Trump banning CNN from the White House is a warning of things to come if Paramount Skydance swallows Warner Bros. (Trump also banned MSNOW and Politico).
	

	“As Trump tries to ban CNN from the White House, it would be a massive mistake to cave on the Paramount merger,” Warren wrote. “The last thing we need is another Trump-controlled media conglomerate abusing its power to stomp out competition. This is a dangerous merger.”
